Volume 08 · Chapter 09

Mergers, acquisitions and control

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v08-c08

By the endEvaluate acquisition economics and distinguish synergy from wealth transfers.

Capability and prerequisites

After this chapter, you can value an acquisition from a dated operating forecast, reconcile the purchase and financing of every claim, and calculate how cash and share offers divide the gains. You can also explain why earnings-per-share accretion, goodwill and an observed takeover premium do not establish buyer value creation. Complete real options and strategic flexibility; retain the cash-flow and claim boundaries of Chapter 2, the reinvestment discipline of Chapter 3 and the comparison tests of Chapter 7.

A board receives a proposal described as “a 21% premium, funded with inexpensive debt, and immediately accretive.” Those descriptions leave the central questions unanswered. What would the target be worth without the acquisition? Which changes require this particular buyer? What must be invested to obtain them? How much value will the sellers receive, including their participation in the merged business? Start with those questions before choosing a payment mechanism.

1. Value the business and identify the claims being purchased

Use one valuation date, immediately after any separately specified distributions and before the proposed closing payments. Let Vop be the value of the specified operating business, C separately available excess cash, H other assets excluded from operations, D debt and O other senior or outside-owner claims. All are market values or explicit conditional estimates on the same basis. Ordinary-equity value is

E = Vop + C + H − D − O.

O can include preference shares, noncontrolling interests, or obligations whose cash costs are excluded from Vop. Match the perimeter: a forecast of 100% of a subsidiary cannot all belong to the parent's shareholders. Required operating cash is already part of the operating investment plan. Leases may be treated as operating payments or financing claims, but cannot be charged fully in both places. These are the same boundaries used in Chapter 7.

An offer to buy all ordinary shares pays the shareholders, not automatically the lenders or preferred owners. If the ordinary-equity consideration is Q, a transaction operating-value convention is Q + D + O − C − H, provided those claims and assets remain inside the acquired perimeter. Report whether debt is assumed, refinanced or retired, and whether the seller withdraws cash before closing. A cash-free, debt-free asset sale is a different contract. Its price cannot be compared directly with a share purchase price without the bridge.

Retirement at a contractual amount different from the debt's existing market value creates a separate effect. A make-whole payment, refinancing fee, lost tax attribute or change in an existing creditor's value belongs in the incremental valuation. Debt principal paid at fair value is an exchange of cash for an extinguished claim; it is not an additional operating loss. Conversely, assuming debt is not free financing.

2. Separate control improvements, combination benefits and transfers

Construct the target's standalone value under a specified credible policy. A control improvement is an incremental change that a capable owner could implement in that business without combining it with this buyer: for example, ending an unprofitable product or repairing collections. The improvement must be feasible and net of its implementation costs. Buyer-specific synergy requires the combination, such as using complementary distribution or eliminating duplicate capacity. Damodaran's control and synergy definitions distinguish the improved standalone counterfactual from the combination counterfactual.

Write down both counterfactuals. If the improved target already closes a redundant depot, the combined forecast cannot count that same closure again. If the incumbent is already implementing the improvement, it belongs in standalone value to the extent already expected. A buyer's claim that management is poor is not a measured cash-flow difference. Similarly, paying below an analyst's estimate may benefit the buyer without the acquisition itself improving operations; disagreement about baseline value is distinct from an incremental combination benefit.

Denote by S the net incremental value available to the two ordinary-shareholder groups, relative to their specified standalone values. Here it includes control improvements and buyer-specific benefits, less incremental investment, integration, transaction and financing costs. Existing outside claimants are held at unchanged fair values unless a separate transfer is included. An operating gain accompanied by a 5 increase in an existing creditor's claim leaves 5 less for ordinary shareholders; that creditor gain must appear in a wider investor reconciliation.

S = PV(control cash improvements) + PV(combination cash benefits)
− PV(incremental investment and integration) − PV(deal costs)
+ net financing side effects − value transferred to other existing claimants.

This is a valuation decomposition, not permission to add overlapping forecasts. An alternative is to value the complete combined cash path and subtract both complete standalone values. The two routes should agree. Finance benefits already embedded in a compatible operating discount rate must not be added again. Additional borrowing proceeds alone create no S because lenders receive a matching fairly priced claim. A tax saving requires an applicable cash-tax calculation, not the word “synergy.”

Private value is not a welfare measure. Higher profits caused by reduced competitive pressure can partly transfer value from customers; renegotiated wages or public subsidies can shift value from other parties. The aggregate shareholder gain defined here does not establish an equal social resource gain. A board should identify affected parties and feasible implementation, even when its immediate valuation question concerns investor claims.

3. Forecast net benefits at the dates when they can occur

Revenue synergy is incremental cash contribution after the costs needed to serve the extra sales, customer losses, cash taxes and investment. Cost savings should allow for replacement services, severance, systems migration and the time needed to close capacity. A full operating forecast can use ΔFCFF = ΔEBIT + ΔD&A − Δcash tax − ΔCapEx − Δworking capital. A direct cash ledger is equally valid when every cash item is supplied. Do not subtract accounting depreciation as a cash payment or omit the asset purchase because its expense is delayed.

Assign each benefit an operational mechanism, responsible owner, start date and evidence. A procurement saving might be linked to contracted quantities and prices; a sales benefit needs a customer conversion and contribution-margin argument. Damodaran's acquisition notes, slides 19–22, connect combination value to the form and timing of the cash-flow change and to reinvestment and returns. The following finite ledger and all its numbers are original.

Worked example 1 — Alder buys Bracken: benefits, price and financing

Alder Process Supply and Bracken Service Systems are fictional businesses, unrelated to earlier cases. Money is in kCU, share counts in thousands, and prices in CU per share. T0 is a hypothetical closing date; T1, T2 and T3 are one, two and three years later. No number is an observed market quote. Baseline values immediately before closing are supplied as internally compatible conditional values. There are no separately excluded holdings or leases, no NCI and no other claims.

The supplied discount rate for every future incremental cash item is 10%; this is a case assumption, not Alder's debt rate or an estimated market rate. After-tax control receipts are 8.25, 9.075 and 9.9825. Each has PV 7.5, so control improvement adds 22.5 to standalone operating value. Bracken under the improved policy would therefore have operating value 262.5 and ordinary equity 212.5, with its other claims unchanged. Buyer-specific after-tax receipts are 33, 36.3 and 39.93. Each has PV 30, giving 90 before the required investment and costs. Integration PV is 12 + 4.4/1.1 = 16. Thus:

S = 22.5 + 90 − 30 − 16 − 6.5 = 60.

The combined funded operations immediately after closing, before financing claims, are worth 630 + 240 + 22.5 + 90 − 4 = 978.5. Only the future integration payment remains in that value. The 30 investment, 12 immediate integration payment and 6.5 fee have already been paid at closing; the sources-and-uses table below accounts for them. Subtracting them again from 978.5 would duplicate the cash outlay.

Alder offers 230 cash for Bracken's ordinary equity, retires its debt at 60 and retains its preferred claim at 10. The operating transaction value convention is 230 + 60 + 10 − 20 = 280. Its 40 excess over standalone operating value 240 equals the equity premium 230−190. The quoted ordinary-equity premium is 40/190 = 21.0526%; the percentage against operating value is different.

The fictional closing contract permits both excess-cash balances to be used simultaneously with the purchase; neither funds operations. A lender offers at most 250 of new debt proceeds on fair terms. No new equity is raised from outsiders, and the financed cases have zero incremental net financing side effects beyond the stated fee. Old Alder debt and Bracken preferred value remain unchanged. These are explicit assumptions about pricing and access, not consequences of the balance sheet.

After closing, excess cash is zero, target debt is gone, and ordinary equity belongs entirely to Alder's old shareholders. Its value is 978.5 − 100 − 248.5 − 10 = 620. They started with 600, so their gain is 20. Sellers receive 230 for a standalone claim worth 190, gaining 40. The gains sum to S = 60. The old lenders and preferred owners neither gain nor lose, and the new lender receives a claim worth its contribution.

4. Derive the cash-price ceiling and distinguish it from a funding limit

Let EA and ET denote standalone buyer and target ordinary-equity values. Under the preceding boundary, a cash payment Q leaves old-buyer equity EA + ET + S − Q. This includes the depletion of buyer cash or the issuance of fairly priced financing claims. Subtracting the buyer's old equity gives

Buyer gain = ET + S − Q;
target gain = Q − ET;
sum of ordinary-shareholder gains = S.

For S ≥ 0, both groups can weakly benefit when ET ≤ Q ≤ ET + S. The buyer's economic ceiling is therefore Qmax = ET + S, conditional on feasible financing and the assumed cash path. It leaves the buyer no incremental gain. A positive buyer hurdle or bargaining advantage calls for a lower price. If S < 0, no price makes both groups better off on these same baseline valuations.

In the case, the economic ceiling is 250, but closing borrowing equals Q + 18.5. With a 250 debt commitment and the specified cash balances, the funding ceiling is 231.5. The proposed 230 clears both tests, with financing slack only 1.5. Paying 250 would require 268.5 of new borrowing or another explicit funding repair. An economic ceiling is not a promise that a lender will finance it. Additional equity issuance would change ownership and could carry its own costs.

Price sensitivity is simple only when S is independent of price. Every extra unit paid to sellers then reduces buyer gain by one and increases target gain by one. If fees depend on price, funding changes tax or distress costs, or a different offer changes integration commitments, recompute S and the claims. The buyer cannot preserve an old S by ignoring those consequences.

5. Price a fixed exchange ratio using post-deal ownership

For a pure share exchange, let nA be old buyer shares, nT old target shares and k the number of newly issued buyer shares delivered per target share. The number issued is x = knT. Assume a single equal-rights ordinary-share class, no other dilution, divisible shares, no cash paid to ordinary sellers and unchanged S under this financing policy. The combined ordinary equity has value EC = EA + ET + S. Then

PC = EC/(nA + x);
target consideration = xPC; old-buyer wealth = nAPC.
Buyer gain = nAPC − EA; target gain = xPC − ET.

The post-deal price is endogenous: issuing more shares divides the same combined equity into more units. The headline xPA, using the old buyer price, is not the actual value transferred unless PC happens to equal PA. Sellers receive part of their own contributed business and part of the combination gain. The buyer is giving away a fraction of the whole combined claim, not paying with an asset whose price can be frozen independently.

Worked example 2 — The same businesses, twelve new shares

Replace the cash offer with k = 1.2 Alder shares for each of Bracken's 10 thousand shares: x = 12 thousand. Keep the same operating plan, investment and fees. Cash uses now total 60 + 30 + 12 + 6.5 = 108.5. The two cash balances provide 90, so new debt is only 18.5. The source-and-use balance is 70 + 20 + 18.5 = 108.5. Bracken's ordinary shares are exchanged and canceled; do not add its old 10 to Alder's 30 and the new 12.

The funded operating value remains 978.5. Combined ordinary equity is 978.5−100−18.5−10 = 850, agreeing with 600+190+60. With 42 thousand shares, price is 425/21 ≈ CU 20.2381. Sellers own 12/42 = 2/7 and receive value 1,700/7 ≈ 242.8571. Old buyer shareholders retain 5/7, worth 4,250/7 ≈ 607.1429. Their gain is 50/7 ≈ 7.1429; target gain is 370/7 ≈ 52.8571. The sum remains 60.

The headline stock offer was 12×20 = 240. Its actual closing value is higher by 20/7 ≈ 2.8571. Relative to the 230 cash offer, more of the 60 goes to sellers, while the combined company borrows less. Lower borrowing does not itself prove higher old-buyer value: payment terms and claim ownership matter.

Derive participation bounds rather than guessing a premium. For positive EA, ET, EA + S and EC, seller participation xEC/(nA+x) ≥ ET gives x(EA+S) ≥ nAET. Buyer participation gives nA(ET+S) ≥ EAx. Thus:

nAET/(EA+S) ≤ x ≤ nA(ET+S)/EA.

The case interval is 95/11 ≈ 8.6364 to 12.5 thousand shares, or exchange ratios 19/22 ≈ 0.8636 to 1.25. At the lower bound the target gets its standalone 190 and the buyer gets all 60. At the upper bound old-buyer value stays 600 and sellers get 250. These are valuation bounds, not a prediction of bargaining outcomes. When S = 0 they coincide; when S < 0 there is no mutually acceptable interval under the stated positive-value conditions.

A fixed-value stock promise is different from a fixed ratio. If sellers must receive Q and the same combined equity value EC applies, then xEC/(nA+x) = Q yields x = nAQ/(EC−Q), requiring 0 ≤ Q < EC. Matching the cash payment 230 requires x = 345/31 ≈ 11.1290, k = 69/62 and PC = 62/3. Then target value is 230 and old-buyer value is 620. Simply issuing 230/20 = 11.5 at the old price would transfer a different amount. Real contracts can specify pricing windows, collars or contingent payments; value their actual rules rather than substituting either simple formula.

6. Make benefit realization and closing risk explicit

For a transparent operating sensitivity, multiply only buyer-specific cash receipts and their associated taxes by f, while holding control improvements, initial investment and integration costs fixed. This is a specified scaling experiment: costs do not disappear because sales disappoint. Then S(f) = 90f−30. Financing at closing is unchanged for a given consideration policy, although actual lenders could change terms if their information changed.

Realization sensitivity under the fixed cash and fixed-ratio offers, kCU except share price
fSCash buyer gainCash target gainStock priceStock buyer gainStock target gain
160204020.23817.142952.8571
0.7537.5−2.54019.7024−8.928646.4286
0.515−254019.1667−2540

For each row, the two gains sum to S. A fixed cash seller exits the modeled operating risk after payment. A fixed-ratio seller retains 2/7 of the combined ordinary claim, receiving 2/7 of a marginal change in S; the old buyer receives 5/7. In this offer, however, sellers initially receive a larger share of value, so risk sharing does not ensure a better buyer outcome. Cash buyer break-even requires f ≥ 7/9; the twelve-share offer requires f ≥ 8/9.

Delay is another dimension. If only the three buyer-specific receipts and their taxes move one year later, their PV falls from 90 to 90/1.1. Keeping all costs at their old dates reduces S to 570/11 ≈ 51.8182, and cash buyer gain to 130/11 ≈ 11.8182. A perpetual synergy assumption would conceal the finite contractual horizon; a delay cannot be valued merely by relabeling the years.

Worked example 3 — Signing is a different decision date

Use a separate illustrative signing decision today, with closing or failure one year later. The case supplies a linear owner planning criterion: weight the two outcomes by physical probabilities and discount their incremental wealth at 5%. The success probability is 3/4. Conditional success creates buyer gain 20 and target gain 40 measured at that later date relative to their same-date standalone alternatives. Failure causes an external buyer cost 4 and external target disruption cost 2. An additional buyer advisory cost 3 is paid today regardless of outcome. These amounts are outside the already valued closing case; none is a transfer between buyer and seller.

The buyer's signing value under the criterion is [(3/4)20−(1/4)4]/1.05−3 = 31/3 ≈ 10.3333. Target value is [(3/4)40−(1/4)2]/1.05 = 590/21 ≈ 28.0952. Their sum is 269/7 ≈ 38.4286, which also equals [(3/4)60−(1/4)6]/1.05−3. Conditional buyer gain 20 is not today's signing value.

At a general success probability p, buyer value is (24p−4)/1.05−3. Break-even is p = 143/480 ≈ 29.7917%. This is a decision threshold under the stipulated owner criterion. Physical probabilities and a discount rate do not independently establish market prices; Chapter 8 explains the additional pricing assumptions. If a break payment ran from one party to the other, it would enter their individual gains with opposite signs and cancel from the combined gain.

Integration feasibility also matters after closing. A team cannot simultaneously deliver incompatible migration schedules, and expected annual savings cannot pay an immediate severance bill. Specify milestones, financing availability, customer retention and a fallback policy. Approval, consent and remedy conditions depend on the actual contract and applicable jurisdiction. No universal legal approval threshold or tax treatment is assumed here.

7. Explain earnings accretion without mistaking it for value

EPS accretion means the chosen post-deal earnings-per-share measure exceeds the comparable standalone measure. It is an accounting ratio test. For a full first year with a share-funded purchase at its beginning, no earnings adjustments and x new shares, post-deal EPS is (NIA+NIT)/(nA+x). If NIA and share counts are positive, multiplication gives the accretion condition nANIT > xNIA. That condition contains neither the target's value nor net synergy.

Worked example 4 — More earnings per share, less buyer wealth

A separate fictional buyer, Fenwick Instruments, has ordinary equity 400, 20 thousand shares and next-year ordinary net income 20. Lowbank Components has equity 100, 10 thousand shares and next-year ordinary net income 10. Values are supplied independently of the one-year earnings numbers and can reflect different risk, growth and investment prospects. There are no debt, tax, acquisition-accounting or fee adjustments in this illustration. No incremental cash benefit is created: S = 0. Fenwick issues 6 thousand equal-rights shares for all target equity at the start of the forecast year.

Combined value is 500, shares 26, and price 250/13 ≈ 19.2308, below Fenwick's old 20. Old buyers retain 20/26 of 500 = 5,000/13 ≈ 384.6154, losing 200/13 ≈ 15.3846. Sellers receive 1,500/13 ≈ 115.3846 and gain the same 200/13. Total gain is zero: the offer transfers value from buyers to sellers.

Yet forecast EPS rises from 20/20 = 1 to 30/26 = 15/13 ≈ 1.1538, a 15.3846% increase. Combined P/E is 500/30 = 50/3 ≈ 16.6667, rather than Fenwick's old 20. Applying 20 to the larger EPS would invent value not present in the cash-flow assumptions. The accretion inequality, 20×10 > 6×20, holds even though buyer wealth falls.

For cash financing, include incremental interest, lost income on spent cash, realistic cash taxes and acquisition-related earnings adjustments in the NI bridge. For a part-year close, use the appropriate weighted-average share count and compatible included earnings period. A reported earnings increase can coexist with a large investment outlay, lower growth or greater risk. Likewise, value-creating investment can initially reduce EPS. Present EPS as a reporting consequence alongside, not as a substitute for, the wealth calculation.

8. Keep accounting, observed premiums and economic judgment distinct

The IFRS Foundation's public IFRS 3 overview, inspected on 8 October 2026, describes recognition and measurement of acquired assets, liabilities and other interests and the allocation to goodwill. It is a framework-specific overview, not a complete transaction ruling. In a deliberately simple 100% purchase with no previously held interest or NCI, suppose recognized consideration is 230 and fair value of identifiable net assets attributable to the purchased claim is 180. The stipulated acquisition allocation gives goodwill 50.

Goodwill 50 is not the case's net S of 60, the seller gain of 40 or the buyer gain of 20. It is a residual in the stated accounting allocation. It can include benefits of an existing business not separately recognized as identifiable assets, expected combination benefits, or an overpayment. Neither its recognition nor a later accounting charge supplies a fresh cash-flow forecast. A bargain-purchase accounting outcome also needs the applicable recognition and reassessment rules; it does not license mechanically declaring a trading profit.

An observed takeover premium compares a consideration value with a selected reference price. Its interpretation depends on the price date, rumors, expected competing bids, information released with the offer and payment terms. If a target's observed price already includes some probability of control improvement, adding the full improvement to that price can count the expectation twice. A fixed-ratio headline premium changes as the buyer price changes. Report the quoted convention and the conditional economic value separately.

A useful evidence packet therefore preserves the unaffected-price rationale, standalone forecasts, full comparable-deal selection rule, claim bridge, consideration contract and timing of public information. Announcement returns reflect revisions in expected outcomes; they do not isolate realized operating synergy without an identification argument. A premium average from selected completed transactions is not a universal control value. Chapter 7's comparability and selection cautions apply here, with the added need to distinguish cash and stock contracts and to retain failed proposals in the research design when relevant.

A defensible board recommendation states the best independent alternative, a price or exchange-ratio limit, the feasible financing, a quantified downside and the evidence that would reverse the decision. Alder's 230 cash offer has modeled buyer gain 20 and only 1.5 funding slack. At 75% realization of buyer-specific benefits, it loses 2.5 even though total shareholder value increases by 37.5. Those two facts support an explicit diligence and financing condition; they do not justify unconditional approval merely because the base case is positive.

9. Reproduce the claims, funding and sensitivity

The offline package contains the original JSON inputs, standard-library Python analysis, exact reference output and instructions and limits. Save the four files together and run python3 v08-c09-analysis.py. Decimal inputs are read as exact rational values; output records fractions, and the printed manuscript rounds only display values. No market data or network access is required.

The lab recomputes each benefit PV, both source-and-use balances, surviving claims, shareholder gains, participation bounds, the equivalent fixed-value offer, realization and delay scenarios, the EPS counterexample and the signing decision. Change the offer or a benefit assumption and follow the claim balance through to each shareholder group. A numerically balanced model can still rest on unsupported benefits or unavailable financing; the checker cannot authenticate those judgments.

Exercises

  1. A target has operating value 360, separately accessible cash 25, an excluded investment worth 15, debt 90 and preferred claims 20. There are 15 thousand ordinary shares. An offer pays 330 for all ordinary equity, with the listed assets and claims in the acquired perimeter. Compute standalone ordinary equity, price per share, the transaction operating-value convention, the premium amount and the equity-premium percentage. Explain why adding debt to the seller's cash proceeds would misstate ordinary-shareholder gain.
  2. Use the Alder–Bracken ledger. Recalculate net S and buyer NPV on the 230 cash offer when only buyer-specific receipts and their taxes are realized at 75%, with every cost and control improvement unchanged. Find the minimum realization fraction for nonnegative cash buyer NPV. Separately, retain full receipts but delay only those buyer-specific receipts and their taxes from T1–T3 to T2–T4; calculate the new S and cash buyer NPV.
  3. Use the baseline Alder–Bracken cash offer and all original closing uses, but reduce the new-debt commitment from 250 to 240. Calculate the financing gap and the highest cash offer financeable without new outside equity or any operating change. At that financeable offer, calculate buyer and target gains. Distinguish this funding ceiling from the original economic ceiling.
  4. Use the baseline share exchange but issue 13 thousand shares instead of 12, keeping S = 60 and the original non-consideration funding. Compute combined equity, price, each group's wealth and gain, and the exchange ratio. Verify that total gain is still S. Derive the maximum number of shares consistent with nonnegative buyer gain and assess the 13-share proposal.
  5. For the baseline S = 60, derive the number of newly issued Alder shares that gives sellers a fixed value of 230. Compute the post-deal price and both groups' gains. Compare this with issuing 230/20 shares based on the old price: calculate the actual consideration under that shortcut. State the positivity condition required by the fixed-value formula.
  6. In the Fenwick–Lowbank EPS case, replace the six-share issue by seven thousand new shares; all other inputs are unchanged. Compute post-deal EPS, percentage accretion, post-deal price, old-buyer wealth and each group's gain. Derive the share threshold for strict EPS accretion and the share threshold for nonnegative buyer value; explain the interval where their signals conflict.
  7. A separate simple 100% acquisition has recognized cash consideration 145, identifiable net assets 110 and no NCI or previous holding. Supplied standalone target equity is 125; net incremental acquisition benefit after all costs is 12. Compute stipulated goodwill, target gain and buyer gain. A director says, “The positive goodwill proves the premium was justified.” Give a logically complete response distinguishing all three quantities, without asserting unprovided accounting or tax rules.
  8. Use the signing case but set success probability to 1/4; keep the buyer's immediate cost 3, failure costs 4 and 2, success gains 20 and 40, and the stated 5% owner criterion. Compute buyer, target and combined signing values. Then evaluate the claim that an industry-average 25% takeover premium establishes both the probability of closing and the value of control. Identify at least four missing pieces of evidence and explain why physical expected-value arithmetic alone does not identify a market price.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria
  1. Standalone ordinary equity is 360+25+15−90−20 = 290; per share it is 290/15 = 58/3 ≈ CU 19.3333. The offer's operating-value convention is 330+90+20−25−15 = 400. Both the operating premium, 400−360, and the equity premium, 330−290, are 40. Relative to ordinary equity, the premium is 40/290 = 4/29 ≈ 13.7931%. The debt claim belongs to lenders, not ordinary sellers. Retiring or assuming it affects the total transaction and financing, but ordinary sellers receive 330 and gain 40 on the supplied baseline.
  2. Control PV remains 22.5, buyer-specific receipt PV becomes 0.75×90 = 67.5, and investment, integration and fees remain 30, 16 and 6.5. Thus S = 37.5 and cash buyer NPV is 190+37.5−230 = −2.5. In general, S(f)=90f−30 and buyer NPV=90f−70, so f ≥ 7/9 ≈ 77.7778%. For the separate delay, buyer-specific PV becomes 90/1.1 = 900/11. Then S = 900/11−30 = 570/11 ≈ 51.8182 and buyer NPV = 570/11−40 = 130/11 ≈ 11.8182. The lost PV is 90−900/11 = 90/11; no other payment was delayed.
  3. Original borrowing need is 248.5, so the reduced commitment leaves 8.5 unfunded. Total non-consideration uses are 60+30+12+6.5 = 108.5, cash sources are 90 and borrowing is at most 240. Therefore Q ≤ 90+240−108.5 = 221.5. At Q = 221.5, target gain is 221.5−190 = 31.5; buyer gain is 190+60−221.5 = 28.5; the sum is 60. The economic ceiling remains 250 under unchanged benefits and fair financing. Raising the price from 221.5 without identifying another source fails the closing cash balance, even when its calculated NPV is positive.
  4. Combined ordinary equity remains 850, with 43 thousand shares and price 850/43 ≈ 19.7674. Old buyers hold value 25,500/43 ≈ 593.0233, so their gain is −300/43 ≈ −6.9767. Sellers hold value 11,050/43 ≈ 256.9767 and gain 2,880/43 ≈ 66.9767. Gains sum to 2,580/43 = 60. The ratio is 13/10 = 1.3. Buyer participation requires 30(190+60) ≥ 600x, hence x ≤ 12.5. Thirteen exceeds that bound, transferring more than all the net acquisition gain to sellers; a positive total S does not rescue the old buyers.
  5. Set x×850/(30+x) = 230. Then 620x = 6,900, giving x = 345/31 ≈ 11.1290 and k = x/10 = 69/62. Price is 850/(30+345/31) = 62/3 ≈ 20.6667. Sellers receive 230 and gain 40; old buyers hold 30×62/3 = 620 and gain 20. The shortcut issues 11.5 shares; its price is 850/41.5 = 1,700/83, giving sellers 11.5×1,700/83 = 19,550/83 ≈ 235.5422, not 230. The formula requires nonnegative Q below positive EC, so EC−Q > 0, as well as positive old-buyer shares. Equal cash-equivalent gains here depend on the stipulated unchanged S; different financing effects require a new comparison.
  6. EPS becomes 30/27 = 10/9 ≈ 1.1111, an increase of 1/9 ≈ 11.1111%. Price is 500/27 ≈ 18.5185. Old buyers retain 20×500/27 = 10,000/27 ≈ 370.3704, losing 800/27 ≈ 29.6296. Sellers hold 3,500/27 and gain 800/27; total gain is zero. Strict EPS accretion requires 20×10 > 20x, or x < 10. Nonnegative old-buyer value requires 20×100 ≥ 400x, or x ≤ 5. For 5 < x < 10, EPS rises while old-buyer wealth falls. Equality at ten gives unchanged EPS; equality at five gives unchanged buyer wealth. Earnings and value weights are different.
  7. The stated allocation gives goodwill 145−110 = 35. Target gain is 145−125 = 20; buyer gain is 125+12−145 = −8. Together they gain 12. The 35 accounting residual compares consideration with identifiable net assets, not with standalone economic equity or the net combination gain. Paying a 20 premium for only 12 of net incremental benefit loses 8 for the buyer under the supplied estimates. The director's inference therefore fails even though goodwill is positive. A complete response identifies the three different comparison bases and does not infer a missing tax benefit from the accounting entry.
  8. Buyer value is [(1/4)20−(3/4)4]/1.05−3 = 40/21−3 = −23/21 ≈ −1.0952. Target value is [(1/4)40−(3/4)2]/1.05 = 170/21 ≈ 8.0952. The sum is 7, also [(1/4)60−(3/4)6]/1.05−3. Buyer acceptance is not justified by the positive combined value. The premium claim is unsupported: an answer should ask for, at minimum, the reference-price date and rumor information; matched standalone/control forecasts; the cash, ratio, collar or contingent consideration terms; the full peer-deal universe including selection and failed bids; and evidence about contractual closing conditions and state-specific losses. Other well-explained items such as claim perimeter or integration capacity earn credit. A percentage paid in selected deals identifies neither a probability nor an incremental cash forecast. Physical probability weights give the stipulated owner calculation; market value additionally needs justified risk pricing or replication, as in Chapter 8.

Teach-back

Explain to a board member, in three minutes, why a 230 cash offer and an offer of shares quoted at 240 are not directly comparable purchase costs. Show the target's 190 standalone equity bridge, the net S = 60 ledger, the two financing balances and the endogenously determined share price. Then give one reason EPS and one reason goodwill cannot settle the acquisition decision.

Teaching benchmark

A complete explanation distinguishes operating value from equity, identifies debt retirement and excess-cash use once, and shows cash buyer gain 20 versus fixed-ratio buyer gain 50/7. The twelve new shares are a 2/7 claim on combined equity 850, so their actual consideration is 1,700/7, not 240. The non-consideration uses still need cash in the stock deal. EPS compares an earnings numerator with a share denominator; goodwill compares recognized consideration with identifiable net assets. Neither substitutes for future net cash and the allocation of its value. Do not call borrowing proceeds a synergy or apply the old buyer price to all new shares without justification.

Delayed check

After several days, without the worked tables: (1) derive the cash buyer-gain identity; (2) derive the share-exchange participation interval; (3) explain how a creditor value increase changes the common-shareholder reconciliation; and (4) reconstruct the financeable cash ceiling with 90 available cash, 108.5 non-consideration uses and a 250 debt commitment.

Retention answers

(1) Old buyer wealth after a cash deal is EA+ET+S−Q, so gain is ET+S−Q; target gain is Q−ET. (2) Use each group's share of EA+ET+S and solve its standalone participation inequality: nAET/(EA+S) ≤ x ≤ nA(ET+S)/EA, under the positive-value conditions stated above. (3) With operating gains unchanged, an increase in an old creditor's claim reduces value available to common owners; include the creditor in the total investor gain rather than treating its gain as new resources. (4) Q+108.5 ≤ 90+250 gives Q ≤ 231.5, even though the case's economic ceiling is 250.

Sources, scope and extension

The linked author-hosted control derivation and acquisition notes support the conceptual counterfactual and timing distinctions. The latter contain historical accounting and company material; this chapter uses only the specified valuation-method passages, not their old accounting choices, historical estimates or a universal exchange-ratio recommendation. The official IFRS overview supports only the scoped acquisition-accounting description. All cases, wealth derivations, sensitivity calculations and problems here are original.

The chapter assumes known claim boundaries and supplied valuation inputs; it does not establish the accuracy of a real target forecast, the availability of real financing or jurisdiction-specific tax and competition outcomes. Deeper work can build a transaction-specific mixed-consideration model with contingent closing and creditor repricing, or an event study with explicit identification and information timing. The following private-equity and venture chapter extends sources and uses into leveraged ownership, financing rounds and fund returns.

Sources and further study

  • Aswath Damodaran — Chapter 25 Discussion Issues and Derivations: Valuing Synergy and Control — Scoped author-hosted definitions of combination value relative to separate firms and control value relative to the status quo. Chapter supplies its own assumptions, original cases, claim-level wealth identities and proof of the share-exchange bounds.
  • Aswath Damodaran — Acquisition Valuation, author-hosted lecture slides — Scoped primary teaching reference for defining the operating mechanism, timing, reinvestment and returns behind combination benefits; slides 19–22. All chapter numbers, finite cash schedules and payment-contract equations are original.
  • IFRS Foundation — IFRS 3 Business Combinations, public overview — Acquisition recognition of identifiable assets/liabilities, noncontrolling interests and goodwill; distinguishes a business from an asset acquisition.
